question: A Claude-assisted case-summary way of working produces good results for the analyst who designed it, but two colleagues get noticeably worse results from the same written instructions. What should the designer do first?
options: A) Add examples of good summaries to the instructions so the expected standard is unmistakable.
B) Rewrite the instructions in much more detail so that less is left to the individual using them.
C) Ask the two colleagues to use the designer's own saved wording word for word every time.
D) Watch each colleague run the work once and see where their inputs differ from the designer's.
correct_answers: D) Watch each colleague run the work once and see where their inputs differ from the designer's.
explanations: Worked examples usually improve an arrangement and may well be part of the eventual fix. Adding them before the divergence has been observed is still a guess at the cause.
More detail is a plausible fix but an untargeted one. Without knowing which part of the colleagues' use diverges, the designer may add paragraphs about something that was never the problem.

Copying the designer's wording exactly hides the difference rather than explaining it, and it will not transfer to the next case. It also suggests the arrangement only works when one person operates it.

Correct. The same instructions producing different results means the difference is in what people actually do with them. Watching one run each is the quickest way to find the unstated step the designer performs without noticing, and it is what makes any later rewrite land in the right place.
